summary: Describes a MIB module for the Digital Video Broadcasting Return Channel via Satellite (DVB-RCS) system as defined by the SatLabs Group. It provides objects for monitoring the behavior and performance of network-layer entities using DVB-RCS. It is informational and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Satellite internet equipment needs a way to report how it is doing. This document defines a list of dials and gauges that a network manager can read.

questions: how to monitor satellite dvb-rcs equipment with snmp
what is a return channel satellite terminal
how does dvb-rcs satellite internet work
subtitle: A standardized way to monitor satellite internet equipment that connects back to the network.

tldr.problem: Satellite operators run thousands of Return Channel Satellite Terminals (RCSTs) in customer homes. These devices need remote monitoring: checking signal strength, tracking traffic, detecting faults. Each vendor implemented proprietary monitoring, making it difficult to manage multi-vendor networks.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB (Management Information Base) defines standard data objects (dials and gauges) that every DVB-RCS terminal must expose via SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). These objects track system status, network configuration, installation state, quality of service, and forward and return link performance.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use a single management station to query any DVB-RCS terminal, regardless of vendor. The SatLabs Group adopted this MIB as a certification requirement for interoperable equipment.

today: RFC 5728 is an Informational document specifying the SatLabs Group DVB-RCS MIB. It has not been obsoleted. The MIB is widely implemented in commercial DVB-RCS equipment and remains the standard for managing these satellite internet systems in operational networks.

sections.title: DVB-RCS Satellite Internet
sections.content:
DVB-RCS (Digital Video Broadcasting Return Channel via Satellite) is a standard for satellite internet. The system works in two directions: a satellite broadcasts television and data to customer terminals (forward link), and customer terminals send requests and traffic back to the satellite (return channel). This is different from one-way satellite broadcasting; it enables interactive services like web browsing and VoIP.

A customer installation consists of an RCST (Return Channel Satellite Terminal): an indoor box (IDU) that connects to a customer's LAN, and an outdoor antenna and receiver (ODU) that talks to the satellite. A Network Control Center (NCC) on the ground manages the satellite and thousands of RCSTs.

The SatLabs Group, an industry consortium founded in 2001, works on interoperability. To certify that different manufacturers' RCSTs work together, SatLabs defined management standards including this MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: A satellite internet antenna in your yard talks to a space satellite that can send and receive data. The company running the satellite needs to know if your antenna is working, how strong the signal is, and how much data you are using.

sections.title: Management Information Base Concepts
sections.content:
A MIB (Management Information Base) is a standardized catalog of data objects. A MIB module is a document that defines objects for a specific type of equipment. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the protocol used to read and write MIB objects over the network.

Each MIB object has a name (like dvbRcsRcstSystemType), a type (integer, string, counter, etc.), and access rights (read-only or read-write). A read-only object reports status; a read-write object allows remote configuration. MIB objects are organized hierarchically into groups (e.g., all system-level objects in one group, all forward-link objects in another).

This MIB module follows the SMI (Structure of Management Information) standard and is compliant with RFC 2578, RFC 2579, and RFC 2580. The module is assigned the object identifier mib-2.transmission.239 by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a menu of things you can ask a device to report: What is your model number? What is the signal strength? How many packets have you sent? Every satellite antenna gives the same answers in the same format.

sections.title: Organizing the MIB
sections.content:
This MIB is divided into several groups. The dvbRcsRcst group covers the terminal itself: system identification, network configuration, installation parameters, quality of service settings, operational control, and current state. The dvbRcsFwdLink group covers the downlink (broadcast from satellite): configuration and status including modulation, coding, and signal quality. The dvbRcsRtnLink group covers the uplink (return to satellite): configuration of traffic classes and bandwidth allocation.

Within the return link group are objects for managing Capacity Categories: CRA (continuous bandwidth), RBDC (dynamic bandwidth based on rate requests), and VBDC/AVBDC (dynamic bandwidth based on volume). These categories determine how much bandwidth the NCC allocates to each terminal based on demand.

Objects track MPEG and ATM traffic profiles, PID pools (packet identifiers for stream multiplexing), Request Classes (traffic classes with different priorities), and performance metrics like packet loss and latency.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB is like a filing cabinet. One drawer holds the antenna's basic info. Another holds dials measuring the signal down from the satellite. Another holds dials measuring the signal up to the satellite. Another tracks how much bandwidth you are using.

sections.title: DVB-RCS Protocols and Standards
sections.content:
DVB-RCS uses DVB-S or DVB-S2 for the forward link. DVB-S (first generation) uses a fixed modulation and coding rate for all terminals receiving the same satellite beam. DVB-S2 (second generation) supports Adaptive Coding and Modulation (ACM): different terminals can receive at different data rates based on their signal quality.

The return link uses TDMA (Time-Division Multiple Access): the satellite assigns each terminal a time slot in which to transmit. The RFC supports both ATM and MPEG transport profiles for formatting bursts of data. Configuration objects in the MIB track which profiles are in use, along with tuning parameters like frequency, modulation index, and power levels.

The MIB includes objects for antenna alignment (during installation), installation logging, and configuration file management (terminals store XML configuration files that can be queried or updated remotely).
sections.plainLanguage: The satellite uses different transmission schemes for sending down (broadcast) and receiving up (time-sharing). The MIB tracks which scheme is in use, what the settings are, and how well it is working.

sections.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
Network operators use this MIB to monitor terminal health. Read-only objects report signal metrics: carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR), bit error rate (BER), and received signal level in dBm. The MIB tracks statistics: packets sent and received, bytes transmitted, errors detected, and capacity requests made to the NCC.

Administrators can set alarms based on thresholds (e.g., alert if signal drops below a minimum). They can trigger diagnostics: continuous wave (CW) frequency measurements during antenna installation, log file retrieval for post-installation troubleshooting. The MIB also allows remote firmware updates and configuration changes.

The relationship to the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863) establishes how DVB-RCS interfaces (MAC layer, TDM, TDMA) stack with IP, MPEG, and ATM layers, allowing integration with general network management tools.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can check: Is the antenna receiving a signal? How strong is it? Are there transmission errors? How much data has passed through? Are there any problems in the log file?

sections.title: Interoperability and Certification
sections.content:
The MIB defines formal Compliance groups. A manufacturer building a certified RCST must support certain MIB objects as a minimum (mandatory groups) and may optionally support others based on the features they implement (optional features). The RFC lists which objects are required for basic functionality, which are required for specific options (like DVB-S2 support), and which are optional enhancements.

By enforcing MIB support at certification, SatLabs ensures that a manager workstation querying any certified RCST gets consistent, predictable responses. This eliminates vendor-specific command sets and allows network operations teams to manage fleets of equipment from multiple suppliers using the same tools and procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: To be certified, a satellite antenna must respond to these standard questions. A manager can use the same software to manage antennas from Company A and Company B.
